agents.blurb: Goes through every recurring charge for price rises you did not notice, services you pay for twice, annual renewals about to land, and charges to things you appear to have stopped using.

agents.blurb: Projects the next 90 days day by day from the commitments already known, finds the date the balance is lowest, and says which charges put it there.
agents.name: Cashflow Sentinel

agents.name: Emergency Fund & Resilience

agents.blurb: Compares the recent months against the same stretch a year ago, category by category, and separates a structural rise - more often, or more each time - from one expensive month.
agents.name: Lifestyle Creep Detector

attribution.default: Its own calendar month. A one-off is NEVER moved.

steps.detail: It has to be monthly and seen at least 3 times. A one-off payment stays in the month it happened, always.
steps.name: Only a monthly series can move at all

steps.detail: Pay landing on the 31st, 1st, 30th and 2nd is one payday either side of a month boundary. A plain median of those days gives the 16th, which is wrong about every one of them; the circular median gives the month end.
steps.name: Its payday is the circular median day

steps.detail: Payday on or after the 24th and it arrives on or before the 6th: that is the PREVIOUS month's pay. Payday on or before the 6th and it arrives on or after the 25th: that is next month's, early.
steps.name: Late arrivals go back, early ones go forward

steps.detail: Shifting can CREATE the double count it exists to prevent: pay on 31 August and again on 1 September, and moving September back lands both in August and empties September. The occurrence nearest payday keeps the month and the other is put back in its own calendar month - moved back, not merely annotated.
steps.name: A series never contributes twice to one month

steps.detail: When no shift can separate them the row is marked for review with the reason, rather than being silently moved to a month it may not belong to.
steps.name: Two genuine payments in one month are flagged, not moved

bureau_matching.note: Bureaus report credit, not deposits. Saying a savings account is missing from your credit report would be noise dressed as a finding.

directions.detail: The strongest signal there is: the statement's own balance column went up or down by exactly this amount. It overrides everything below, because it is the bank's arithmetic rather than a reading of its wording.
directions.label: The running balance moved this way

directions.detail: The statement has separate columns for money in and money out, and this amount was printed in one of them. Nothing needs inferring.
directions.label: It was in the debit / credit column

directions.detail: The statement printed the direction next to the figure. Only one amount column, but the cell annotates itself.
directions.label: The amount itself said CR or DR

directions.detail: The statement carries a Dr/Cr or Deposit/Withdrawal column and this row's said which.
directions.label: A type column said so

directions.detail: The one narration whose meaning flips with the account it is on: money arriving on the card, money leaving the bank account funding it. Read as an outgoing on both sides, every bill payment would be counted twice.
directions.label: It reads as a credit card bill payment

directions.detail: A single-amount-column statement carries no position to read, so the narration decides. Weakest of the real signals, and the reason explicit outgoing words are checked before a coincidental credit word.
directions.label: The wording says so

directions.detail: One amount column, no marker, no type column, and wording that settles nothing. The row is worth checking - this is the assumption that, left uncorrected, once booked every salary credit as spending.
directions.label: Nothing said, so money out was assumed

Someone repaying a purchase made on your card. Subtracted from spending rather than added to income - the purchase is already counted.
Moved into an investment. Still your money, so not spending.

pairing.name: A transfer between your own accounts
pairing.note: Same amount to within 0.01, at most 4 days apart, and it must cross accounts. Neither leg counts as income or spending.

pairing.name: A failed charge and its own reversal
pairing.note: One debit, a same-amount credit and often a second debit, on ONE account within 3 days. That is one failed attempt and one that went through, not three events.

pairing.name: The same row arriving on two statements
pairing.note: Matched on account, date, amount and direction, with the running balance required to agree - two identical payments in one afternoon are possible. A narration that is a strict prefix of another is one row two extractions cut at different lengths; the fuller one survives.

pairing.name: A card bill settled across several legs
pairing.note: Only attempted when the bank leg independently names a payment rail. Bounded to 12 candidates and 5 legs a side, and below 0.5 confidence it goes to review rather than applying itself.

recurring.amount_note: A charge whose price ROSE is still one charge: a clean level shift keeps the series and the new level becomes the going-forward figure. So does a steady drift, which is what a loan's interest component does every month for twenty years.
recurring.note: Grouped by a merchant signature with numbers, month names and rail codes stripped, then every cadence is FITTED to the dates and the best-scoring one wins. The score weighs how close the dates sit to the rhythm they claim, how tightly they cluster on one day of the month, how many periods in the span actually hold a charge, and whether any period holds two - which is proof the rhythm is wrong.

model.instructions:
You categorize bank and credit-card transaction descriptions.

You will be given a numbered list of merchant strings from Indian bank
statements. For each, choose exactly one category from the allowed list.

Rules:
- Return ONLY a JSON array. No prose, no code fences.
- One object per input: {"i": <index>, "category": "<category>", "confidence": <0..1>}
- Use "uncategorized" when the string is genuinely uninformative (a bare
  reference number, an unreadable code). Do NOT guess to fill the list.
- Descriptions are payment-rail strings, so they are abbreviated and noisy.
- "direction" tells you whether money came in or went out; a credit is far more
  likely to be income, a refund, or a reversal.
- The "emi" category means a LENDER collecting a loan instalment, and nothing
  else. Card issuers print the word "EMI" against ordinary purchases purely to
  advertise that the charge could be split into instalments if the cardholder
  asked - nothing was borrowed and the full price was paid, exactly like any
  other purchase. Those markers have already been removed from the strings
  below, so if you still see one treat it as noise and categorise by the
  merchant: a hospital is healthcare, a school is education, an electronics
  shop is shopping.
- Never answer "emi", "loan_interest" or "cc_payment" for a string that only
  names a merchant. Those three describe who is being repaid, and a merchant
  name is not evidence of a debt.
never_used_for: Any figure. Every total, balance, payoff date and forecast is arithmetic over your own rows.
Deciding direction, pairing transfers, or reconciling a statement.

Anything at all unless you switch it on - it is off by default, and the switch lives on the server rather than in the browser so that the thing deciding whether to spend money is the thing that would spend it.
used_for: Naming a merchant that no rule recognises.
Writing the plain-English summary on the dashboard.
Filling identity fields a statement's letterhead did not yield.

forecast.band_note: Every month carries a low, expected and high figure rather than one number. The band is never narrower than this share of the median month: four near-identical months would otherwise produce a band of almost nothing, which reads as a promise next month cannot keep.

confidence.needs: 6+ months of history, 3+ active recurring series, and spending varying by less than 25%

forecast.limits: It projects your EXISTING patterns forward. It knows nothing about a job change, a bonus, a medical event or inflation, and says so on the screen.
forecast.note: Built from two parts with very different certainty. Committed money is recurring series already detected - the EMI will leave on the 5th. Everything else is modelled from your own observed month-to-month variance. No model is asked to guess a figure.

loans.note: Every number is a closed-form formula, never a model. A loan's future is fully determined by principal, rate and EMI - there is nothing to predict, only to calculate. Asking a model for a payoff date would be inventing uncertainty where none exists.
loans.rate_recovery: Where a statement does not print the interest rate, it is recovered from the interest actually charged rather than guessed.

classification_order.test: A bureau is named AND at least two of: credit report, credit information, credit score, account information, enquiry, CIR.
Not a record of trades, then an ISIN alone is proof - otherwise two softer markers must agree.
Everything else. Last on purpose: it is the only reader with a reconciliation gate to catch its own mistakes.

formats.note: The file's first bytes decide, not its extension. People rename files, and mail clients hand out .xls files that are really HTML - trusting the extension is how you get "no tables found" on a perfectly good statement.

jobs.note: A job that reaches one of these never changes again, so the screen stops asking. Work survives a restart: progress is written through as it happens rather than held in memory until the end.

stages.name: Remove duplicates
stages.why: Before anything pairs rows together. A duplicate matched against its own original would hide both.

stages.name: Filter parser artifacts
stages.why: A misread row is dropped here rather than being categorised, paired and forecast on.

stages.name: Cancel reversed charges
stages.why: A failed charge and its refund are one non-event.

stages.name: Match transfers between accounts
stages.why: So money you moved is not counted as income and spending.

stages.name: Match card settlements
stages.why: The multi-leg cases 1:1 pairing cannot reach.

stages.name: Categorise
stages.why: Rules first; the model only for what rules left over, and only if you turned it on.

stages.name: Consult learned categories
stages.why: A merchant you have already corrected keeps your answer.

privacy.note: Applied to every narration before a model sees it. The model is off unless you turn it on in Settings; this is what it would receive if you did.

removed.why: Yours and the payee's - a UPI handle is an email address.
Indian mobile numbers appear inside UPI narrations.
Card statements print the merchant's locality, which can identify where you live.
A person you paid is not a merchant.

fallbacks: The masked account or card number, with the account type.
The card's own product name, for an issuer that masks its number so completely no digit survives extraction.
Institution and account type together, as a last resort.
account_identity.note: Whether two statements describe the SAME account. The masked number plus the account type settles it on its own - the institution is deliberately left out of the key, because the same account exported twice can disagree about it when one file's letterhead names the bank and another's does not.
account_identity.why_it_matters: Treating that disagreement as two accounts silently doubles income, spending and investments - the worst failure this app can have, because every figure still looks plausible.

account_number.fallback: If no label matches, a masked number printed on its own is used - and failing that, the institution and account type together.

labels.label: Card Number
labels.means: The card's own number. Always wins - a card statement that also prints an account number is naming two different things.

labels.label: A/C Number
labels.means: The abbreviated form of the same.

labels.label: Membership Number
labels.means: What some issuers call a card.

never.label: Customer ID / Cust ID / CRN / CKYC
never.why: One customer ID covers every account the bank holds for you. ICICI prints the account number plainly some months and only the Cust ID on others; reading the ID as an account number filed half of one salary account's statements under XXXX9341 and half under XXXX1951, double-counting every overlapping month.

never.label: Alternate / secondary / previous / linked / former
never.why: A qualifier that demotes the label after it. "Alternate Account Number" names a real field, but not the one that identifies the account.

account_number.note: Which number on a statement identifies the account. The labels are tried in this order and the first that matches wins, so the ORDER is the rule.
account_number.shapes_first: Amex prints XXXX-XXXXXX-31004, which no label search would find, so that shape is matched before any label is tried.
account_number.stored_as: Only the last four digits are ever kept. Enough to tell two accounts apart, useless to anyone who reads the database.

read.not_a_transaction: \b(?:will be|would be|is due|due on|reminder|scheduled|has failed|failed|declined|unsuccessful|statement is ready|e-?statement|your otp is|is your otp|your verification code|use otp|auto[- ]?pay (?:is )?(?:set|scheduled))\b

person_vs_business.note: Money sent to a named individual is the bulk of Indian UPI and is not shopping. It is categorised separately so spending totals mean what they say.
signals: A company token in the name - Ltd, Pvt, Enterprises, Store, Services and the like - makes it a business.
An honorific (Mr, Mrs, Shri, Smt, Dr) makes it a person.
Otherwise, a payee that is two to four capitalised words and nothing else reads as a person's name.

scopes.note: Totals, forecasts and recurring series. Reproducible from the parsed ledger in seconds.
The ledger itself - transactions, accounts, statements. Rebuildable from the statement files.
The statement files themselves. Anything from Gmail could be downloaded again; anything uploaded by hand exists nowhere else.
Documents read but not yet processed. Clearing these loses no ledger.
What a rebuild replaces, which deliberately excludes the job telling you it is running.
What a model suggested. Always regenerable, and never the same twice.
What YOU decided. Cannot be regenerated by anything.

storage.snapshot_note: Every clearing action takes a snapshot first, so none of them is final.

thresholds.name: Minimum columns for a table
thresholds.why: Rows narrower than this are page furniture, not data.

thresholds.name: Dated rows before we stop looking
thresholds.why: Below this, the slower stream extraction is worth running as well in case it finds a better table.

thresholds.name: Rows that make a transaction table
thresholds.why: One is permitted: a genuinely quiet month has a single transaction, and a candidate must already map to date, description and amount to get this far.

thresholds.name: Letterhead window
thresholds.why: Identity is read from the top of the document only. A savings statement's body says HOME LOAN EMI on every EMI row, and matching that relabels the whole account.

thresholds.name: Footer window kept
thresholds.why: Totals sometimes sit in a footer, so the tail is kept and everything between is dropped.

thresholds.name: Password candidates tried
thresholds.why: A hard cap. These are published formats, not guesses - a brute-force space for an eight-character password is about 10^14 - and the cap guarantees a large profile cannot turn this into a brute-forcer.

thresholds.name: Balance tolerance
thresholds.why: Statements round to paise and a few institutions publish totals to the rupee, so a sub-rupee gap is not evidence of a bug.

thresholds.name: Material discrepancy
thresholds.why: Above this we stop calling it a rounding artefact and call it a broken parse.

thresholds.name: Days apart
thresholds.why: NEFT and IMPS settle same-day, but a weekend or a card issuer's posting lag can stretch it.

thresholds.name: Amount tolerance
thresholds.why: Transfers move an exact figure. Anything looser starts pairing unrelated transactions of similar size.

thresholds.name: Days apart
thresholds.why: Wider than a plain transfer's window - card issuers post with more lag.

thresholds.name: Residual allowed (absolute)
thresholds.why: A multi-leg group need not tally to the paise; the remainder is usually a wallet top-up or rounding.

thresholds.name: Candidates considered
thresholds.why: Subset-sum over a whole ledger will find coincidences, so the search is bounded to the nearest few by date.

thresholds.name: Confidence floor
thresholds.why: Below this a group goes to review rather than applying itself. One leg matching one leg on an exact amount is strong evidence; five legs summing to a sixth is what a large ledger produces on its own.

thresholds.name: Auto-link confidence
thresholds.why: Nothing auto-links on a lender's name alone.

thresholds.name: Amount may vary by
thresholds.why: The default. Utilities drift a lot month to month and a subscription barely moves, so the tolerance is set per category - an EMI is the same to the paisa, an electricity bill triples between March and June and is no less a fixed obligation.

thresholds.name: Cadence fit floor
thresholds.why: Every cadence is fitted to the dates and the best one wins. Below this, nothing fits: the charges keep no rhythm, whatever their amounts do.

thresholds.name: Price change to notice
thresholds.why: A jump smaller than this is noise. A bigger one - with both levels tight and every charge cleanly on one side of it - is a price rise, and the series survives it with the new level as the going-forward figure.

thresholds.name: Supersede window
thresholds.why: How close a statement row must be to an alert to be considered the same payment. The statement always wins: it is checked, the alert is not.

03b41acb-74fd-4b17-91fa-c9659a5cb47b.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN t.direction = 'debit' THEN CAST(ROUND(CAST(t.amount AS REAL) * 100) AS INTEGER) ELSE 0 END) AS m0 FROM transactions t LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id WHERE CASE WHEN t.accounting_month IS NOT NULL AND t.accounting_month != '' THEN t.accounting_month ELSE substr(t.txn_date, 1, 7) END >= ? AND CASE WHEN t.accounting_month IS NOT NULL AND t.accounting_month != '' THEN t.accounting_month ELSE substr(t.txn_date, 1, 7) END <= ? AND CASE WHEN t.flow_role != '' THEN t.flow_role ELSE 'unassigned' END IN (?) AND t.is_mirror_leg = 0 AND t.excluded = 0 LIMIT 201
